title: AI Daily Brief - 2026-06-18
tags:
  - applied-ai
---

## Today in One Minute

- Google is rolling out Gemini and NotebookLM to more universities, with new examples of how higher-education staff and students are using them for studying, research, and course design.
- OpenAI published research on a near-autonomous "AI chemist" that improved a difficult medicinal chemistry reaction, alongside a new LifeSciBench benchmark for testing AI in life sciences tasks.
- A Towards Data Science piece argues that most teams building AI assistants do not actually need a heavy "agent framework" and can get further with simple Python and direct API calls.

## What Happened

- Google's education post highlights how universities are embedding Gemini and NotebookLM into teaching and learning, including AI-assisted study guides, research summarisation, and staff-built notebooks for course content.
- OpenAI describes an AI system that planned, ran, and refined chemistry experiments with minimal human steering to improve yield on a hard reaction, and separately introduced LifeSciBench, a benchmark for evaluating AI on biology and chemistry tasks.
- The Towards Data Science article "You Probably Don't Need an Agent Framework" shows that many agent use cases can be built with plain function calls, loops, and standard libraries, and that frameworks often add complexity without clear benefit.

## Why It Matters

- The Google education update is directly relevant to RP lecturers: NotebookLM-style tools can speed up lesson prep, generate study aids from lecture notes, and give students structured ways to revise, which fits naturally into diploma teaching.
- The AI chemist and LifeSciBench work matters for Applied Science, Pharmaceutical Science, and related diplomas because it shows how AI is starting to assist real lab decisions, and it gives a concrete talking point about how AI in science is evaluated.
- The "no agent framework needed" piece matters for IT and AI students who are tempted to jump straight to LangChain or similar tools. Understanding when plain code is enough builds stronger fundamentals and avoids unnecessary dependencies in student projects.

## Try This Today

- Open NotebookLM in Edge on your Windows 11 laptop, upload one week of your lecture slides or notes, and ask it to produce a study guide and 5 quiz questions. Check the output for accuracy before considering it for class use.
- Ask Copilot or ChatGPT to explain, in simple terms, how the OpenAI AI chemist decided which experiments to run next, then write a 3-sentence summary you could share with a science class.
- Take a small student "agent" idea (for example, an assistant that summarises an article and emails it) and sketch it in plain Python pseudocode without any agent framework, listing only the function calls you would actually need.

## Teaching Angle

- Run a 15-minute classroom demo comparing a NotebookLM-generated study guide with a student's own notes, and discuss what AI got right, what it missed, and what this means for revision habits.
- For science or health-related diplomas, use the AI chemist story as a discussion starter: where should a human still make the final call in a lab, and what risks come with letting AI propose experiments?
- For IT or AI modules, set a short exercise where students must justify whether their project really needs an "agent framework" or can be built with simple scripts, using the Towards Data Science argument as a prompt for debate.

## Links

- [How universities are preparing students for an AI-powered future](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/higher-education-gemini-notebooklm/)
- [A near-autonomous AI chemist improves a challenging reaction in medicinal chemistry](https://openai.com/index/ai-chemist-improves-reaction)
- [Introducing LifeSciBench](https://openai.com/index/introducing-life-sci-bench)
- [You Probably Don't Need an Agent Framework](https://towardsdatascience.com/you-probably-dont-need-an-agent-framework/)
